newsitem.title: UK: British election overshadowed on markets by France.
newsitem.headline: British election overshadowed on markets by France.

text.p: Britain's election campaign has generated a deluge of media coverage and even a few policy initiatives but for financial markets it pales in comparison with the vote looming on the other side of the Channel.
The snap election called by French President Jacques Chirac last week, to be held in two rounds on May 25 and June 1, could help to decide the fate of a single European currency.

Despite the strong possibility that British voters may end 18 years of Conservative rule and elect a Labour government on May 1, the British election appears a mere sideshow in terms of its international economic significance.
"The French election is far, far more important for the markets than Britain's," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW.

In calling the election, Chirac is seeking a mandate for the centre-right coalition of Prime Minister Alain Juppe to continue the harsh economic measures needed to prepare for a single European currency.
Hopes for European economic and monetary union depend on a twin axis of Germany and France pushing it through on time in January 1999.

Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber International, sees it in stark terms. "If the incumbent government win a new term of office, EMU remains on track. If they don't, it doesn't.
"If you don't have France, you don't have EMU and that spells a serious risk for the markets."
To gauge EMU's power over the markets, look no further than Italy. Early in 1995, when it was assumed Italy would not make the first round of a single currency, the German mark was worth 1,265 lira.
Now, Italy is thought a possible EMU entrant and its currency has firmed. One mark now buys just 990 lira.
Similarly, 10-year Italian government bonds used to yield 650 basis points more than 10-year German Bunds. That premium has now dwindled to just 180 points.

Britain's election could have some implications for European integration but both main parties are sitting on the fence over EMU -- both the Labour and Conservative Parties retain an open option on joining.
Tony Blair's Labour Party, which has a strong lead in opinion polls, is viewed by some as more pro-European than John Major's Conservatives.
Labour would sign the European Union's Social Chapter on minimum employment rights and a directive limiting working hours. But it still hedges its bets on the single currency.

In France, the centre-right backs EMU all the way but the Socialists have adopted an "EMU, but not any price" stance. It is that clear water between the parties, and the possibility of a left-wing win, which has the markets fretting.

France has been plunged into recession as Chirac and Juppe have adopted an austere fiscal regime in order to cut their budget deficit to three percent of national income demanded of EMU entrants by the Maastricht criteria.
In the process, unemployment has soared to record levels of about 13 percent of the workforce.
The outgoing coalition enjoyed a huge 464-seat majority in parliament, but early opinion polls suggest it has a razor-thin lead over the Socialists.
Economists at Goldman Sachs put the odds on an election victory for the Chirac/Juppe axis at 60 percent and a win for the left wing at 40 percent.

"Left-wing parties will run the election on a strongly anti-austerity platform," the investment bank said in a note to clients. "Officially, the Socialist Party would not be ready to tighten French fiscal policy even if this is needed to reach the three percent Maastricht target in 1997."
On Monday, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said he would put conditions on entering the single currency, adding a flexible view of the three percent budget deficit target should be taken.

Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking, said the Socialists would steer clear of any measure likely to put up unemployment further. "They won't tie themselves to the Maastricht criteria in the way Juppe would do."
In contrast, the only thing that could put the UK election back on the markets' map would be a narrowing of Labour's lead.

There was a sharp intake of breath last week when one poll slashed Labour's lead to five points from 14. But jitters proved short-lived and the FTSE-100 index of leading UK shares ended the day 50 points higher.
Other polls since then put the opposition 15 to 24 points ahead, pointing to a Labour lansdlide.

It may seem odd for traditionally Tory-supporting financial markets in the City of London to hope for a Labour victory -- in 1992, when John Major pulled off a surprise election win champagne corks were heard popping in the Square Mile for days.
But the one thing markets dread above all else is uncertainty and nothing would be more uncertain than a "hung parliament" in which no party had a clear majority.
"A hung parliament would be a nightmare scenario but it doesn't look likely," one futures trader said.

In the final analysis, the French election may prove to be good news for European markets too. "Our view is we will see the incumbent government win by a comfortable margin, albeit much reduced," O'Hanlon said. "EMU will remain on track."
But until that happens, there will be a lot of sweaty palms.
